definition: Tiny living things that use sunlight to make food. Some can make toxins. They are also called blue-green algae, but they are bacteria.
A layer of organisms growing on the bottom. Pieces can break loose and float up.
A large increase in algae or cyanobacteria. More growth does not always mean more toxins.
A poison made by a living thing. A photo or water colour cannot tell us whether toxins are present.
A blue pigment in many cyanobacteria. A sensor can look for its signal, but that signal does not prove toxins are present.
A green pigment used to capture light. It is found in cyanobacteria and many other organisms that use sunlight.
A substance living things need to grow, such as nitrogen or phosphorus.
Oxygen mixed into water. Fish and many other water animals need it.
How cloudy water is because of tiny floating particles. Mud and living things can both make water cloudy.
A number that tells how acidic or basic water is.
Water moving past a place. River discharge measures how much water passes in a set time.
One small part of an image. A satellite pixel may mix signals from water, land and plants.
A pixel that covers more than one kind of surface, such as a narrow lake and its shore.
A simplified way to describe a system. Models leave things out, so we need to test them.
An example made with a model. It is not a measurement of the real lake.
A guess about the future based on evidence and a method. It can be wrong.
A prediction of an event that does not happen, using the event definition in that test.
Examples saved for testing a model. The model does not use these examples while learning.
The smallest amount a test can reliably report. Below this limit does not always mean zero.
The area of land that drains water toward a stream, river or lake.
A saved copy of data from a certain time. It does not update itself.
A picture taken through a microscope.
Observations or measurements that help us check an idea.
